This vignette shows how to display cortical geometry, curvature, and vertex
values with RGL. It uses the small `std.8` surfaces bundled with neurosurf
(642 vertices per hemisphere), so no downloads are needed. Every RGL scene
below is embedded as an interactive WebGL widget: drag to rotate, scroll to
zoom. The static figure uses neurosurf's CPU renderer, which needs no OpenGL.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%")
```

```{r load}
library(neurosurf)
fs <- load_fsaverage_std8("smoothwm")
inflated_lh <- load_fsaverage_std8("inflated")$lh
left <- smooth(fs$lh, type = "HCLaplace", delta = 0.2, iteration = 5)
right <- smooth(fs$rh, type = "HCLaplace", delta = 0.2, iteration = 5)
curv <- curvature(left)
```

For values, two smooth clusters of opposite sign stand in for a statistic map.
Each is placed at a surface coordinate and falls off with distance over the
inflated surface, which follows the cortical sheet:

```{r values}
blob <- function(centre, peak, width = 18) {
  seed <- which.min(colSums((t(coords(left)) - centre)^2))
  xyz <- coords(inflated_lh)
  peak * exp(-colSums((t(xyz) - xyz[seed, ])^2) / (2 * width^2))
}
vertex_values <- blob(c(-45, -60, 20), 3) +  # parietal, positive
  blob(c(-55, -20, 0), -2.5)                 # temporal, negative
```

Signed values need a diverging palette. `surface_palette()` returns the one
neurosurf uses for static figures and widgets: blue below zero, red above,
with no white centre to fade into the grey anatomy. It is the default
whenever the colour range spans zero; it is named here only to make the
choice visible.

```{r palette}
diverging <- surface_palette("two_sided")
```

## Open a scene and show it

`view_surface()` draws into the current RGL device when `new_window = FALSE`.
This helper gives each example a private NULL device, returns the scene as a
WebGL widget, and closes the device even if the plotting call fails. In an
interactive session, use `rgl::open3d()` to get a desktop window instead.

```{r scene-helper}
with_rgl_scene <- function(code) {
  device <- rgl::open3d(useNULL = TRUE)
  on.exit(rgl::close3d(device), add = TRUE)
  force(code)
  rgl::rglwidget()
}
```

A `SurfaceGeometry` records its hemisphere, so `viewpoint = "lateral"`
selects the appropriate left or right view. By default the surface is shaded
by its curvature, sulci dark and gyri light; `bgcol` replaces that base
colour.

```{r basic-plot}
with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, viewpoint = "lateral", new_window = FALSE)
)
```

## Overlay values

Pass vertex values in `vals`. `irange` sets the colour limits and
`thresh = c(-1, 1)` leaves values inside that band uncoloured, so the
curvature shows through. Each vector has one entry per vertex.

```{r data-overlay}
with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, vals = vertex_values, cmap = diverging,
               irange = c(-3, 3), thresh = c(-1, 1),
               viewpoint = "lateral", new_window = FALSE)
)
```

For a static figure with a colour key, use `surface_figure()`. It renders
with the CPU renderer, so its lighting and colour mapping do not depend on
RGL; this is a rendering of the same values, not a screenshot of the scene
above.

```{r static-overlay}
figure <- surface_figure(
  lh = left, values = vertex_values, anatomy = curv, views = "lateral",
  threshold = 1, limits = c(-3, 3), legend_title = "value",
  panel_width = 640, panel_height = 400, antialias = 2
)
```

```{r overlay-image, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center"}
file <- knitr::fig_path("overlay.png")
dir.create(dirname(file), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_surface_figure(figure, file)
knitr::include_graphics(file)
```

## Vertex colours and transparency

`vert_clrs` supplies explicit colours and overrides scalar colour mapping.
`alpha` sets opacity. Here the anterior half of the hemisphere (positive y)
is one colour and the posterior half another, drawn at 60% opacity.

```{r vertex-colors}
y <- coords(left)[, 2]
halves <- ifelse(y > median(y), "#1b7837", "#762a83")
with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, vert_clrs = halves, alpha = 0.6,
               viewpoint = "lateral", new_window = FALSE)
)
```

`specular` sets the highlight colour (the default `"black"` gives a matte
surface), and `lit` turns lighting on or off. These change the displayed
scene, not the stored geometry or vertex data.

## Combine hemispheres in one scene

Supported views include `"lateral"`, `"medial"`, `"ventral"`, and
`"posterior"`. The two lateral surfaces face opposite directions, so show
them in separate panels. A posterior view sees both hemispheres at once, so
they can share one scene; `offset` separates them along x.

```{r two-hemispheres}
with_rgl_scene({
  view_surface(left, viewpoint = "posterior", offset = c(-5, 0, 0),
               new_window = FALSE)
  view_surface(right, viewpoint = "posterior", offset = c(5, 0, 0),
               new_window = FALSE)
})
```

For static multi-view output, `surface_figure()` combines hemispheres and
labels each view. See `vignette("surface-figures")`.

## Mark vertices

Markers refer to vertices, with a radius and colour for each. These mark
the peak vertex of each cluster:

```{r spheres}
peaks <- c(which.max(vertex_values), which.min(vertex_values))
markers <- data.frame(vertex = peaks, radius = 3,
                      color = c("#b2182b", "#2166ac"))
with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, spheres = markers, spheres_as_vertices = TRUE,
               viewpoint = "lateral", new_window = FALSE)
)
```

## Plot a surface data object

`NeuroSurface` stores values with their vertex indices. Its `plot()` method
passes them to the same rendering machinery, so colour limits, threshold,
opacity, and viewpoint can be set in the call.

```{r surface-object}
surface <- NeuroSurface(left, indices = nodes(left), data = vertex_values)
with_rgl_scene(
  plot(surface, irange = c(-3, 3), thresh = c(-1, 1),
       viewpoint = "lateral", new_window = FALSE)
)
```

## Smooth and threshold a noisy map

Smoothing and cluster-size thresholding operate on surface data before
rendering. Here independent noise at every vertex is averaged over a
20 mm geodesic radius (`sigma`; this mesh's edges are about 10 mm long, so
the radius must span a few of them). Values within 1.5 standard deviations
of zero are then dropped, and only connected clusters of at least 5 vertices
are kept. This illustrates the workflow; it is not an inference.

```{r activation-map}
set.seed(123)
noise <- NeuroSurface(left, indices = nodes(left),
                      data = rnorm(length(nodes(left))))
smoothed <- smooth(noise, sigma = 20)
cut <- 1.5 * sd(smoothed@data)
clustered <- cluster_threshold(smoothed, size = 5,
                               threshold = c(-cut, cut))
with_rgl_scene(
  plot(clustered, irange = c(-2, 2) * cut, thresh = c(-cut, cut),
       viewpoint = "lateral", new_window = FALSE)
)
```

`surface_montage()` arranges several surfaces or `list(surface,
...overrides)` panels from RGL snapshots, so it needs a rendering backend:

```{r montage, eval=FALSE}
surface_montage(
  list(noise, smoothed, list(clustered, thresh = c(-cut, cut))),
  irange = c(-2, 2) * cut, ncol = 3
)
```

## Save an RGL snapshot

`snapshot_surface()` saves a PNG through the available RGL rendering backend.
On a NULL device it needs webshot2 and a headless browser, and it returns an
empty path when no snapshot could be made. Building this article does not
launch a browser, so this recipe is not run here:

```{r snapshot, eval=FALSE}
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
path <- snapshot_surface(left, file = file, vals = vertex_values,
                         cmap = diverging, irange = c(-3, 3),
                         viewpoint = "lateral")
```

For browser-free PNG output, use `surface_figure()` or
`render_surface_rgba()`. For interactive reports with several selectable
maps, see `vignette("interactive-surfaces")`.

The bundled templates retain the FreeSurfer terms in
`system.file("extdata", "LICENSE-FreeSurfer.txt", package = "neurosurf")`.
